sources.cite: NIMH, Ask Suicide-Screening Questions (ASQ) Toolkit, information sheet: four questions and a fifth acuity question asked after any yes; a yes to it is an acute positive, 'imminent risk', that needs a STAT safety and full mental health evaluation, and the patient 'cannot leave until evaluated for safety'; a non-acute positive needs a brief suicide safety assessment; refusing to answer counts as positive
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in NIMH's PDF (summarizing fetch with short quotes). The four questions: a wish to be dead, feeling others would be better off, thoughts of suicide in the past week, any attempt ever. 'Clinical judgment can always override a negative screen.' Validated for youth and adult medical patients, including adult medical inpatients (Horowitz et al., Psychosomatics 2020); the toolkit has emergency department, inpatient and outpatient pathways (NIMH adult toolkit page, read the same day). The questions are paraphrased in the sim.

sources.cite: NIMH, Adult ASQ Toolkit: Brief Suicide Safety Assessment guides, nursing scripts and suicide risk screening pathways for the emergency department, the inpatient medical/surgical unit and outpatient primary care and specialty clinics
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch): an index page; the pathways themselves were not opened, so what each setting does after a positive screen is taken from the information sheet.

sources.cite: The Joint Commission, R3 Report Issue 18: National Patient Safety Goal for suicide prevention, NPSG.15.01.01 (effective 2019-07-01): EP1 environmental risk assessment; EP2 screen 'using a validated screening tool'; EP3 an assessment that 'directly asks about suicidal ideation, plan, intent, suicidal or self-harm behaviors'; EP4 document the risk level and the mitigation plan; EP5-EP7 policies for monitoring, discharge counseling and follow-up
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes; issue dated 2019-11-20, updated 2025-12-03). The report names one-to-one monitoring as a key protocol on nonpsychiatric units; it does not itself require it, so the observation level in each sim is the facility's policy.

brief.situation: Andre Lucero, 34 (a fictional client), is at a community health clinic for a follow-up of his blood pressure. While you take his vital signs (blood pressure 162/98, pulse 112), he says he lost his warehouse job two weeks ago and got an eviction notice this morning. He is gripping the notice and says, 'I don't see a way out. I really don't.' His partner and their 4-year-old live with him. You are the licensed practical nurse rooming him; the RN and the nurse practitioner are both in clinic. You have about 25 minutes before the nurse practitioner comes in.
handover: Hypertension follow-up; out of his blood pressure medicine for a week.

Clinic policy: any statement of hopelessness or wish to die is screened, and any positive answer is reported to the RN or provider at once; the client is not left alone until they see him. A social worker is on site on weekdays.
howItWorks: Choose what to say and do from the action groups. Andre answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the clock by the minutes that exchange took.
His trust, distress and how much he discloses change with what you say. Your role is to stay, keep him safe, collect data and report.
Your time ends at 25 minutes. Afterward you write a short summary, then document what you found and what you did.

source.note: About 25 minutes of rooming time before the nurse practitioner comes in (author's scenario timing).
How trust and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a patient.

effects.log: You put the cuff down, sit at eye level and tell him you are listening.

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)

effects.finding: He nods hard. "Yeah. Like the walls are closing in."

normalize.label: Ground him: 'Let's slow down. One breath. We'll take it one piece at a time.'

effects.log: You slow your own voice, breathe with him and tell him you will take it one piece at a time.

effects.finding: He unclenches his hand a little.

screen.why: He has answered; go on to the follow-up questions.

then.finding: "I've wished I could just disappear. Not killing myself, no. Never tried." Only the first question is yes.

then.log: Positive screen on the first question (a wish to be dead or disappear); no to the other three.

then.finding: "I'm fine. Just do my blood pressure." (Not yet enough trust to answer honestly.)

formulation.question: Write your summary for the RN: what makes this a crisis, what you found, and what you did.

parts.label: Crisis and data
parts.criteria: Names an acute crisis (job loss, eviction notice today, overwhelmed, high blood pressure and pulse, out of medicine) and a non-acute positive screen: a passive wish to disappear, no current thoughts, no attempt, no thoughts of harming others; his partner, child and cousin.
parts.modelAnswer: An acute crisis: he lost his job two weeks ago and got an eviction notice today; he is overwhelmed, his blood pressure is 162/98 with a pulse of 112, and he is out of his medicine. The screen is a non-acute positive: a wish to disappear, no thoughts of killing himself now, no attempt and no thoughts of harming others. His partner, child and cousin are supports.

parts.label: Actions
parts.criteria: Names staying with him, grounding, the screen, reporting to the RN at once, the social worker today, 988 saved, and no promise outside the role.
parts.modelAnswer: I stayed and slowed things down, screened, reported to the RN at once from the room, asked the social worker to see him today about housing and saved 988 in his phone with him. I did not promise what the clinic cannot do.

scoring.modelReasoning: Within the practical nurse's role, crisis intervention means: stay, slow things down, ask directly about suicide and harm to others, keep the client with staff, report to the RN at once and connect help for the most urgent problem. A passive wish to disappear is a positive screen that the RN or provider assesses before he leaves.
